A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that helps websites load faster. Normally, a website's files live in one place, called the origin server — the original computer that stores the real, master copy of everything. If every visitor around the world had to fetch data from that single server, loading would be slow for anyone far away. A CDN solves this by copying popular files to many other computers, called edge locations, positioned closer to visitors in different regions. When someone requests a page, the network checks whether a nearby edge location already has a saved copy; if it does, that's called a cache hit, and the file is delivered instantly from nearby instead of traveling across the world. Think of it like a chain of bakeries that all sell bread from one central recipe, so customers grab a fresh loaf from the shop down the street instead of driving to the one original bakery in a distant town. If no nearby copy exists, the request quietly travels back to the origin server, fetches the file, and often stores a copy closer by for next time. This setup keeps websites fast, reduces strain on the origin server, and helps pages stay available even when traffic surges.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the master files | It's the ultimate source of truth for the website |
| Edge location | A nearby computer holding copies of popular content | It shortens the distance data has to travel |
| Cache hit | When a nearby copy is found and used | It means faster loading and less waiting |
| CDN | The overall network connecting origin and edge locations | It keeps websites fast and reliable worldwide |
